lines: Three teams look at the same freshness promise and propose three completely different ways to build it.
One wants to process every event the instant it arrives. One wants to run everything once an hour. One splits the difference, running every few minutes.
All three are aiming at the same target. Which one actually hits it for the least money?
The always-on option clears that target with room to spare, every single time.
Does having the most room to spare make it the obvious winner, or is there a cheaper option that still clears the bar?
And is there one more question, about redoing old work later, that could flip the answer entirely?
answer: Room to spare isn't free. It's infrastructure running continuously, whether or not the promise actually needs that much margin.
The real rule is: among everything that clears the bar, the cheapest one wins.
One thing can still flip that choice — how expensive it is to redo old output later, once the code that produced it changes.

lines: Picture every option laid out against that one promised ceiling, as a bar each one either clears or doesn't.
An option whose bar sits above the ceiling is finished immediately. No amount of tuning moves a hard physical floor.
What's left afterward is a much shorter list than the one you started with.
Among the options still standing, the always-on one and the two-system hybrid both clear the bar too — just at a steeper running cost.
The option that only checks in every few minutes clears the same bar for noticeably less money.
Of everything still standing, that's the one that should actually win.
Two named answers to one shared problem live on this same card.
One answer keeps two separate systems running side by side, forever, so that redoing old work is already fast whenever it's needed.
The other answer keeps just one system, and redoes old work by rerunning that same job from a saved history of everything that happened.
A newer kind of engine chases that second answer's simplicity, without anyone having to hand-build the rerun logic themselves.
Running two systems side by side sounds like a compute problem, but by the account of the person who named this trade-off, it almost never is.
The real cost is keeping two completely different pieces of code producing the exact same answer, forever, as both keep changing.
The single-system answer pays a different, more honest cost: whenever it redoes old work, it briefly needs roughly twice its usual storage, until that run finishes.
Every place data enters this system from somewhere else makes its own separate choice.
Either the other side sends data over on its own schedule, and owns getting that delivery right.
Or this pipeline reaches out and asks for it, and from that moment on, this pipeline owns whatever goes wrong with that asking.
Say the side that gets asked for data simply has nothing new to report today, for reasons nobody yet knows.
Does the request that asked for it come back looking broken, the way a crash would?
Or does it come back looking exactly like any other day where genuinely nothing happened?
answer: It comes back looking exactly like nothing happened — because, as far as the request is concerned, nothing did.
The request itself reports success either way. It asked, and it got told there was nothing new.
Only something watching how long it's been since fresh data last showed up can tell a real failure apart from an ordinary quiet stretch.

lines: One shared promise, one card, and the cheapest option that still clears it wins — not the one with the most spare room.
Two named answers to redoing old work sit on that card too, each paying its own honest cost rather than a free one.
And every place data comes in from elsewhere makes its own quiet choice about who finds out first when it stops.
Now a brand new request shows up, one that needs an answer in moments rather than minutes, to catch fraud before it ships.
Does shrinking the few-minutes option down far enough still get there in time?
Or does only the always-on option survive this much stricter version of the same promise?
answer: Only the always-on option survives. Checking in periodically, no matter how often, carries its own floor it can never shrink past.
And with nothing slower left as a fallback, the question about how expensive it is to redo old work now matters far more than it used to.
